Um, no, not really. I mean, when you say "acting on impulse," I think of people who, like, jump out of planes or suddenly buy a sports car or, I don't know, quit their job in a blaze of glory or something. And that's definitely not me. I'm actually pretty risk-averse, all things considered.

Well, outside of work... I mean, I guess I kind of just touched on that, right? Like, at home, things are pretty low-stakes. But if you're asking about organizing my time in general, I think where it really, really hits me is actually back at work, to be honest. It's just like, a pile of auto claims here, some property damage ones over there, and then I've got sticky notes stuck to the edges of my monitor, on the bezel, you know? And half the time the sticky notes lose their stickiness and fall onto the keyboard, and I don't even know which file they were supposed to go with. 

And my inbox is even worse. I try to use the little red flags in Outlook, but then I end up flagging everything, so the flags mean nothing. I'll have fifty flagged emails, and when I sit down in the morning with my coffee, I just stare at the screen. I literally have no idea which policy review I'm supposed to tackle first. Should I do the oldest one? The one with the highest payout? The one from the adjuster who called and yelled at me yesterday? I spend so much time just trying to figure out where to start that I end up wasting an hour just clicking between different windows and shuffling folders around. So, yeah, organizing my time and my tasks... it's a huge, huge struggle, but mostly when I have all these competing priorities at the office. Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because with all this stuff happening at work with Brenda and the performance coaching, it really got me thinking about when I was younger. Because, honestly, looking back... this whole thing with missing details and falling behind? It's not actually brand new for me. Like, I remember back in elementary school—specifically, I think it was third or fourth grade, Mrs. Gable's class, she had this whole system with color-coded folders that was supposed to keep us organized, but it just completely backfired for me. 

My parents actually kept a bunch of my old report cards in this big plastic bin in their basement, and I was looking through them a while ago. And it's almost comical, really, because every single year, the comments from the teachers were practically identical. They'd always start with something nice, like, "He's a bright boy," or "He contributes great ideas during group discussions," but then there was always the "but." It was always, "but he loses his worksheets," or "he has trouble keeping track of his assignments." 

I remember I would shove papers into my desk instead of putting them in my backpack, and by the end of the semester, my desk was just a crumpled, overflowing mess of half-finished math sheets and spelling tests. And the teachers were constantly writing notes home saying that I missed instructions. Like, they'd explain a project, and I'd be looking right at them, but my brain was just... somewhere else, maybe thinking about a book I was reading or staring at a bug on the window. And then everyone would start working, and I'd just be sitting there, completely lost, having to ask the kid next to me what we were supposed to be doing.
